title: Rails-style string shaping, without the Ruby
description: Inflector brings the string-shaping toolkit that Rails and ActiveSupport made famous into DuckDB SQL: convert between naming conventions, pluralize and singularize English words, and rewrite struct keys or whole result sets in one call — without dropping into Python or writing a UDF. The transforms are mechanical and deterministic, which is exactly what column-naming and ETL normalization want. What that mechanical, English-centric design does *not* handle is the part worth reading first.

sections.title: Caveats — read these first
sections.description: Inflector is intentionally a rule engine, not a linguist. The transforms are mechanical and English-only, which is the right trade-off for naming work but a trap if you expect semantic or multilingual behavior.

bulletPoints.label: Pluralization is English-only
bulletPoints.description: Singular/plural rules come from the upstream [`cruet`](https://crates.io/crates/cruet) crate, whose ruleset and irregular-word table are English. It handles real English irregulars well — `person` ↔ `people`, `mouse` ↔ `mice`, `analysis` ↔ `analyses` — but has no awareness of French, German, Spanish, or any other language. Non-English input silently produces mechanical English-rule output. For multilingual content, inflect upstream and store the result.

bulletPoints.label: Case transforms are mechanical, not semantic
bulletPoints.description: The tokenizer treats acronyms as runs of capitals, so `inflector_to_snake_case('XMLHttpRequest')` yields `xml_http_request`. That is correct for column-naming work; if you need acronym-preservation rules tuned to your domain, do that step in application code first.

bulletPoints.label: Pluralization isn't always reversible
bulletPoints.description: `people` → `person` round-trips fine, but English has true ambiguities — `data` is both singular and plural in modern usage, and `species` and `series` are unchanged. Don't round-trip a value through plural-then-singular and assume identity.

bulletPoints.label: Single-character tokens are skipped
bulletPoints.description: The case tokenizer requires a two-character minimum and ignores 1-character runs, which matters for inputs like `aB` or single-letter prefixes — those tokens are dropped rather than preserved.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: Inflector is a thin DuckDB binding over the [`cruet`](https://crates.io/crates/cruet) and [`convert_case`](https://crates.io/crates/convert_case) Rust crates — the same Rails / ActiveSupport-Inflector heritage, exposed through DuckDB's function system. The interesting part is not the catalog of helpers (those are enumerated in the Function Reference below) but the dispatch model: how the same conceptual operation is reached three different ways depending on what you're transforming.

bulletPoints.label: Upstream provenance
bulletPoints.description: The actual rule engine — case tokenization, pluralization, the irregular-word tables, the ActiveSupport-style helpers — lives in [`cruet`](https://crates.io/crates/cruet) and [`convert_case`](https://crates.io/crates/convert_case). Inflector is a binding layer that surfaces those crates as DuckDB functions, so behavior tracks the upstream crates rather than being reimplemented.

bulletPoints.label: Scalar functions for a known target
bulletPoints.description: When the target case is known at parse time, there's a dedicated scalar function per case, plus a matching `is_*` predicate for routing a value based on its current shape. String in, string out — vectorized like any other DuckDB scalar.

bulletPoints.label: One polymorphic dispatcher across shapes
bulletPoints.description: [`inflect`](#inflect) takes the case as a runtime argument and is polymorphic on its payload: a `VARCHAR` returns a transformed string, a `STRUCT` returns the same struct with every key renamed (values untouched), and a parenthesized query becomes a table function that rewrites every column name. Same function, three shapes — the headline path for normalizing a whole result set in one call.

sections.title: Inflector vs. RapidFuzz
sections.description: Both extensions live in the Matching & casing group, but they answer different questions — and the line between them is clean.

bulletPoints.label: Inflector: deterministic transformation
bulletPoints.description: Reach for Inflector when you know exactly what shape you want — `snake_case`, `kebab-case`, plural, a foreign-key name — and need to mechanically produce it from a single input. The output is fully determined by the input and the chosen rule.

bulletPoints.label: RapidFuzz: fuzzy comparison
bulletPoints.description: Reach for [`rapidfuzz`](/products/extensions/rapidfuzz) when you have *two* strings and want a similarity score — record linkage, dedupe, spell-check. That's comparison, not transformation. The two compose well: normalize naming with Inflector, then fuzzy-match across the normalized values with RapidFuzz.
